question: When machines arrive to do part of a human language job, as in 1954 and 1966 and today, does the work disappear, or does it change into something people still do?

issues.note: Hard cut from the library reading room to an empty courtroom with a caption 'a few years later: a trial'. The frames do not show who the interpreters are or establish Nuremberg. The place only becomes clear later, and the 1945 date contradicts 'a few years later'.

Cut from the interpreter booth to the lamplighter on the street with the narration 'The lamplighter walks on'. The metaphor is never explained by the picture, and the film jumps from the 1940s booths into the 1954 computer scene.
Abrupt jump from the 1954 computer hall to the 1966 office. The narration 'In 1966' lands on a quiet office with no link back to the forecast.
The split-screen '1966 postediting / today: post-editing' wipe cuts to a wide empty office. The narration about the change showing up in the job market has no matching visual.
Cut from the video-call office to the street at dusk with the caption '1954: a few years'. The look changes abruptly and the callback to 1954 is not set up visually.
The 1954 demonstration is hard to follow because the computer hall shot barely changes for several consecutive frames.
The Nuremberg booth and courtroom views repeat across R03.5 to R04.4 (about 20 s). The same room is shown with little new to look at.
The 1966 office and typewriter scene continues for R13.4 to R14.3 (about 40 s) with very little change.
The remote-interpreter video-call shot lingers across R16.4 to R17.2 with only small variation.
